taste.name: Green means you can press it
taste.trigger: When the designers had a brand green and a page full of links, alerts and dates
taste.decision: Chose to spend the green only on navigation and links over spreading it across headings, icons and backgrounds as decoration
taste.reason: A reader who is unsure of a website needs one dependable rule. If green always means this goes somewhere, they stop testing things with the cursor.
evidence: #006546 on 44 interactive elements and 37 link texts
red #E31C3D kept for one service alert

taste.name: Say the action in a sentence
taste.trigger: When the designers needed calls to action on eleven cards
taste.decision: Chose underlined text links that name the result over filled buttons with short labels, and left out button fills, icon-only controls and hover effects
taste.reason: A person filling in a government form on a slow connection trusts words more than shapes. A sentence cannot be misread the way a Submit button or an icon can.
evidence: 12+ underlined 700-weight links with a circled arrow
only two filled buttons on the page, both in forms

taste.name: Make the reading size the big size
taste.trigger: When the designers set the type scale
taste.decision: Chose an 18px body with a modest 38px headline over a small body under a very large display headline
taste.reason: The audience reads the paragraph, not the slogan, often outdoors or past fifty, so the size goes into ordinary sentences.
evidence: 18px is the most frequent size (37 uses) with 28px line-height

taste.name: One container, learned once
taste.trigger: When the designers had news, dates, tools, topics and blog posts to hold
taste.decision: Chose one white card with a 2px corner and a single gray shadow for all of them over a different treatment per content type
taste.reason: Every new kind of box is something to work out. With one box, attention goes to what is inside it.
evidence: only variation is an 80x6px colored bar on two cards
